title: What the homepage has to prove for a B2B SaaS company
metaTitle: What a B2B SaaS homepage must prove
excerpt: An operator who already runs software needs the homepage to show the product doing a job and a way to book a demo. A feature grid with no job fails that test.
alt: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp. The article is about what a homepage has to prove in that first glance.
caption: The first screen is judged at a working desk, often with something else open beside it. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a B2B SaaS homepage show first?
faqs.answer: Show the product doing a job the buyer already has, and show a way to book a demo. Both should be visible without scrolling. A stranger should be able to name the job and find the booking path after a short look.

faqs.question: Why does a feature grid fail this buyer?
faqs.answer: An operator who already runs software can read a screen and cannot use a tile labeled with an abstract noun. Equal tiles hide which capability is the job. Put one real screen first, and keep any list for later, tied to that job.

faqs.question: Where should the demo sit on the page?
faqs.answer: Put a single demo action in the first view, with a label that says it is a demo. Repeat it at the end if the page is long. Say what the meeting is, so the button is not a surprise form.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A B2B SaaS company homepage has one job for an operator who already runs software: show the product doing a real job, then offer a way to book a demo. Both have to be visible without a scroll. If a stranger can name the job and see the booking path, the page has proved enough to earn the next minute.

A feature grid with no job fails this buyer. Tiles named automation, insights, and collaboration describe a catalog, not a product in use. Operators already live inside software. They are checking whether this tool does a job they recognize, and whether they can see it with someone who will answer questions.

## The buyer already has software

This visitor is not discovering the category. They run a CRM, a billing tool, a support inbox, or a stack of all three. They open your homepage between meetings, often with the product they already pay for still in another tab. The comparison is quiet. Does this replace a step they hate, or does it add a login?

Write for that comparison. Name the job in the words they use on Monday. "Close the books without exporting three spreadsheets" is a job. "Unlock operational excellence" is a poster. The operator can test the first sentence against their week. They cannot test the second, so they leave.

Assume competence. Skip a primer on what software is. Skip a history of the industry. Spend the first lines on the job, the screen where the job happens, and the demo. The rest of the company can wait on later pages.

The same person may be a founder, a head of operations, or the lead who has to approve the tool. They share a habit. They want to see the thing work before they want to hear the company talk about itself. A homepage that leads with a team photo has answered a question they have not asked yet.

## Show the product in use

The picture that carries the page is a real screen, cropped so the job is readable. A queue with a status. A record with the field that matters. A report that names the period. The interface can be simplified for the photograph. It should still be a screen the product ships, not a fantasy layout drawn for the ad.

Put that screen where the first view can hold it, beside or under the sentence that names the job. The sentence and the picture should agree. If the line says the product routes approvals, the screen should show an approval, not a dashboard of equal-sized charts.

Google's Core Web Vitals guidance treats Largest Contentful Paint as the loading measure for the main content, and a good experience means that content paints within 2.5 seconds of the page starting to load. When the product screen is the largest thing in view, a slow image is a failed introduction. The operator did not come to watch a skeleton.

A short line under the screen can name the job in plain words. "A manager approves the invoice without leaving the queue." That sentence does more work than a badge that says trusted by teams. For this buyer, trust is the feeling that the pixels match the claim.

If the product has more than one job, pick the one this homepage is for. A second job can live further down, as a second screen with its own sentence. The first view gets one. A page that tries to be the whole product in the hero is a page that has not chosen a buyer.

## The demo is the action

One path should book a demo. Label it with the words the buyer expects. "Book a demo" is clear. "Get started" is fog when the next step is a calendar, and it is a disappointment when the next step is a sales form with ten fields.

Place the action where the first screen can hold it on a phone. Repeat it at the end of the page if the page is long. In the opening, once is enough. A second competing button, such as a video or a manifesto, splits a decision that was already small.

Say what the demo is. A short meeting. The product on their kind of data, or a walkthrough of a real account with names removed. Who will be on the call. What they should bring, if anything. An operator will book when the next step is described. They stall when the button hides a surprise.

Curiosity can scroll. Commitment gets a button with a plain label. A short section below can show two more screens for the person who is not ready to book. The booking path stays the commitment. Do not bury it under a newsletter field.

## What a feature grid gets wrong

A grid feels complete in a design review. Each tile was a hard-won capability. On the homepage it flattens them into equal weight. The operator cannot tell which tile is the product and which is a setting.

The failure has a recognizable shape. The tiles use internal names. The icons are interchangeable. None of the tiles shows a screen. The grid sits above the product, so the visitor meets the catalog before the job. That order says the company is prouder of the list than of the work.

You can keep a short list later, after the product has been seen. Three lines, each tied to a job, beat twelve tiles. "Routes approvals to the person who owns the budget" is a feature with a job attached. "Workflows" is a tile.

If a salesperson needs the grid for a conversation, put it in the sales deck. The homepage is the minute before the deck, and it has a different job. The deck can be thorough. The homepage has to be choosy.

## Write the page in this order

Use this order and keep a favorite section from jumping the queue.

1. A sentence that names the job and the buyer.
2. A screen of the product doing that job.
3. A way to book a demo, with a label that says so.
4. Two or three proofs that match the same job. A constraint you handled. A kind of team. A before-and-after in the workflow. Skip a logo wall you cannot explain.
5. The limits. Who the product is not for. What it does not replace.
6. The demo again, for the person who scrolled.

The limits belong on the page. An operator trusts a product that says it is for finance teams under a certain complexity, and that it is the wrong fit for a consumer app. A page that claims every industry has not chosen.

Nielsen Norman Group's review of how long people stay on web pages is the reason the order is strict. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and the first 10 seconds are when they decide whether to stay. The job, the screen, and the demo have to land inside that window. Steps four through six are for the person who stayed. In that same account, once someone has stayed for about half a minute, there is a fair chance they will stay much longer. Earn the half minute with the product. Spend it on proof and limits.

## How to test it with an operator

You do not need a research panel. You need someone who runs software and did not write the page.

Open the live page on a phone. Give them about ten seconds. Hide it. Ask what the product does, and what they would click if they wanted a demo. If they answer with a category word and no job, the sentence is still a slogan. If they describe the job and then hunt for the action, the booking path is too quiet.

Ask a second question after they have scrolled. What would this replace in their week? If they cannot point at a step, the screens are decoration. Change the picture before you add another section.

Read the page out loud without the layout. The first three sentences should survive on their own. If they only work beside a gradient, they are not sentences yet. Fix the words before you commission another illustration.

When the homepage is doing this job, the next page the same buyer opens is usually price. They want the shape of the offer before they book. Read [how a pricing page shows fit for this buyer](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-b2b-saas-company) before you hide the numbers behind a form.

When you want the homepage built in that order, with the product visible and a demo path that is honest, look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services).

## What to leave off the first view

Leave the origin story for the about page, and only if it changes a buying decision. Leave an award line you cannot source. Leave a carousel. A carousel spends the opening seconds on a rotation the visitor did not ask for.

Leave the full navigation debate for its own pass, and still keep the header from swallowing the job. A bar of eight products, a search field, and a login can push the product screen below the fold on a laptop. Login can stay. The marketing links can be fewer.

Leave stock photography of a glass office and a laptop you cannot read. If the photograph does not show the product, it is a pause, not evidence. The type, the spacing, and the care of the real screen can carry the taste. A second headline does not need to announce it.

The page can be short. A short page that shows the product in use and books a demo will do more for this buyer than a long page that performs completeness. Completeness is a feeling the team wants. The operator wants a job they can see.
